explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The LORD says, “They will overflow the land and its fullness, the cities and their inhabitants.” The cities are named right there in the picture. So the torrent doesn't leave them alone.

That's right, friend. The torrent doesn't stop at open land. The LORD says it will overflow “…the land and its fullness, the cities and their inhabitants.” The cities and the people living in them are right in the picture.
That's it, friend. The LORD says, “The people will cry out, and all who dwell in the land will wail” It isn't only a few folks, either. All who dwell in the land are in that sentence.

No ships in this verse, friend. The text says the people cry out and all who dwell in the land wail. I can barely get my own mustache through a doorway, so I'm in no shape to race anybody to a dock anyway.

The text doesn't show anybody lining up to fight, friend. What it does say is that “The people will cry out, and all who dwell in the land will wail” That's the whole reaction in this verse. Crying out and wailing, not battle plans.

You heard it right, friend. The wailing comes at the sound of “…the galloping hooves of stallions, the rumbling of chariots, and the clatter of their wheels.” That's three sounds stacked up in one line. Hooves, rumbling and clattering, all headed their way.

That sounds like it would fit the water picture, friend. But the verse names different sounds. It says “…the galloping hooves of stallions, the rumbling of chariots, and the clatter of their wheels.” So the people are hearing horses and chariots, not thunder.

Good guess for a noisy city, friend. But neither crowds nor gates are in this verse. The text lists “…the galloping hooves of stallions, the rumbling of chariots, and the clatter of their wheels.” Hooves and wheels are the sounds that set the wailing off.
It goes the other way, friend. The text says, “The fathers will not turn back for their sons; their hands will hang limp.” So no fathers turn back for their sons. That's a hard line to read.

That's right, friend, and it's a sober one. The LORD says, “The fathers will not turn back for their sons; their hands will hang limp.” The fathers don't turn back, and their hands hang limp. I'll just let that line sit for a second.

Yes, friend. The text says, “Indeed, the LORD is about to destroy the Philistines…” The whole word in this passage comes from Him. It begins with “This is what the LORD says…” and it stays His word all the way through.

No king of Moab shows up in this passage, friend. The verse names who is doing the destroying: “…the LORD is about to destroy the Philistines…” That's the answer straight from the text. I'd keep my eyes on the LORD here, not on a king.

Tyre is in the verse, friend, but not as the one doing the destroying. The text says every remaining ally is cut off from Tyre and Sidon. Then it says who is acting: “…the LORD is about to destroy the Philistines…” So Tyre is on the receiving end of that line.
Right, friend. The text says, “The people of Gaza will shave their heads in mourning…” This is a day of grief for them. I think this one hurts, so I'll let the verse speak for itself.
No party in Gaza, friend. The verse says the people will shave their heads in mourning. It's a sad scene, and I think it's a heavy one. Mourning is the word that fits the blank.

Gaza isn't winning anything in this verse, friend. The text says, “The people of Gaza will shave their heads in mourning…” Mourning is the word, and it's a heavy one. Victory belongs in a different kind of story.

That's right, friend. The LORD says, “Ashkelon will be silenced.” Ashkelon comes up again at the end of the passage too, where the LORD has appointed the sword against it (Jeremiah 47:7). It's a city the word keeps coming back to.

It's actually in the text, friend. Right after Gaza's mourning, the LORD says, “Ashkelon will be silenced.” So Ashkelon doesn't get passed over. The last verse names it again, where the LORD appoints the sword against it and the shore of its coastland.

explanations.answer: Go back in its sheath and be still
explanations.explanation: That's the cry, friend. It says, “Return to your sheath; cease and be still!” It sounds like a plea for the sword to stop. And the very next verse answers it, so keep listening.

explanations.answer: Strike once more and finish fast
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of the cry, friend. The line begs the sword to stop, saying, “Return to your sheath; cease and be still!” Nobody in that line is asking for one more strike. It's a plea to put the sword away.
Egypt isn't in this line, friend. The cry asks the sword, “Return to your sheath; cease and be still!” There's no pointing it somewhere else. The ask is for the sword to stop.
Yes, friend. The verse asks, “How can it rest when the LORD has commanded it?” The sword's work comes from His command. That's the answer to the plea in the verse before.

Sharpened is a fair guess for a sword, friend, but the verse doesn't say that. It says, “How can it rest when the LORD has commanded it?” The word is commanded. I know a thing or two about edges, and I'm still going with what the text says.

Blessed is a warm word, friend, but it's not the one in this verse. The text asks, “How can it rest when the LORD has commanded it?” The sword stays at work because of what the LORD commanded. Now, if I tried to fill that blank with a cozy word, I'd be the one needing a blessing. Commanded is the word that fits.
